text: It decides three things: whether the gradient survives many layers ( saturation ), whether units can switch off for good ( dead units ), and, at the output, what the numbers mean ( probabilities, or a value ).

text: In 2026 the answer for hidden layers of a language model is a gated unit, almost always SwiGLU; GELU survives in vision transformers and older encoders; the ReLU family in convolutional networks and a few efficiency-minded LLMs; sigmoid and tanh only inside gates and at outputs.

section: why a nonlinearity, and what it must be
text: Why a nonlinearity, and what it must be Non-linear, or the stack collapses: W 2 ( W 1 x ) = ( W 2 W 1 ) x , one linear map however many layers there are.
label: core
key: one linear map however many layers

section: why a nonlinearity, and what it must be
text: Not a polynomial, which is the precise condition for a one-hidden-layer network to approximate any continuous function: "a standard multilayer feedforward network with a locally bounded piecewise continuous activation function can approximate any continuous function to any degree of accuracy if and only if the network's activation function is not a polynomial" ( Leshno, Lin, Pinkus and Schocken 1993 ). x 2 alone would not do; squared ReLU, max(0, x ) 2 , is piecewise and is not a polynomial, so it qualifies.
label: depth
key: locally bounded piecewise continuous activation function

section: why a nonlinearity, and what it must be
text: Differentiable almost everywhere is enough for gradient descent: ReLU has no derivative at exactly 0 and frameworks simply pick one (PyTorch's autograd uses 0 there; this page's derivatives agree with autograd everywhere else, src/recompute.py ).
label: core

section: why a nonlinearity, and what it must be
text: Everything else is a trade between four properties: slope near 1 over a wide range (gradients survive depth), outputs centred on zero (updates do not zig-zag), cheap to compute, and smooth (the optimiser sees a smooth surface).
label: core
key: Everything else is a trade between four properties

section: why a nonlinearity, and what it must be
text: No function has all four; the history below is the field trading one for another.
label: fat

text: Sigmoid and tanh: saturation Activation Formula Range Largest slope Good at Trouble Sigmoid σ 1 / (1 + e − x ) (0, 1) 0.25, at x = 0 an output read as a probability; a gate that opens between 0 and 1 saturates on both sides; outputs always positive, not zero-centred Tanh tanh x = 2σ(2 x ) − 1 (−1, 1) 1, at x = 0 zero-centred: outputs, and so the next layer's updates, can have either sign still saturates: slope below 0.01 once | x | > 3.0 derived Saturation.
label: core

text: Backpropagation multiplies the gradient by the activation's slope at every layer.
label: core
key: Backpropagation multiplies the gradient by the activation's

text: A sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so even at its best a gradient shrinks by 4 per layer, and in a saturated unit (| x | large) the slope is close to 0: the slope of the sigmoid is below 0.01 once | x | > 4.6 derived from σ(1 − σ) = 0.01 .
label: core

text: On the parent's "one batch through five networks", the first layer of the 16-layer sigmoid network receives a gradient about 2 billion times smaller than the last (step 2 of the Reading tab of Topic: ml-fundamentals ).
label: core

text: Tanh is a rescaled sigmoid (the identity above), with four times the slope at 0, which is why it was preferred for hidden layers before ReLU.
label: core

text: A unit's weight gradient is its input times one shared error term.
label: core
key: input times one shared error term

text: If every input is positive (a sigmoid layer's output always is), every weight of that unit moves in the same direction at each step, so reaching a target that needs some weights up and others down takes a zig-zag.
label: core

text: LeCun et al. recommend inputs with mean close to zero for this reason, and a scaled tanh, 1.7159 tanh(2 x /3), for hidden units ( Efficient BackProp, 1998 , sections 4.3 and 4.4).
label: core

text: Where they still live.
label: fat

text: Inside gates, where a value between 0 and 1 is the point: the LSTM's forget, input and output gates are sigmoids and its cell candidate a tanh ( Sequence models: the pre-transformer lineage ); the gated units below are this idea moved into the feed-forward block.
label: core
key: forget, input and output gates are sigmoids

text: And at the output, for a binary or multilabel probability.
label: core
key: for a binary or multilabel probability

text: The ReLU family ReLU, max(0, x ), has slope exactly 1 for every positive input, so the gradient passes through any number of active layers unshrunk, and it costs one comparison.
label: core

text: It entered deep learning through restricted Boltzmann machines ( Nair and Hinton 2010 ) and deep supervised networks ( Glorot, Bordes and Bengio 2011 , who stressed that it makes representations sparse: many units output exactly 0).
label: depth

text: AlexNet made it the default: a four-layer convolutional network with ReLUs reached 25% training error on CIFAR-10 six times faster than the same network with tanh ( Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton 2012 , section 3.1).
label: core
key: six times faster than the same network with tanh

text: Its variants each patch one weakness: Variant Formula, for x ≤ 0 (all are x for x > 0 unless said) What it fixes, and its cost Source Leaky ReLU α x , α fixed (0.01 in the paper and PyTorch's default) a small gradient for negative inputs, so a unit cannot be stuck at zero gradient; one more hyperparameter Maas, Hannun and Ng 2013 PReLU a x , a learned (per channel or shared), initialised at 0.25 the network picks the slope; He initialisation was derived for it in the same paper He et al.
label: core

text: 2015 ELU α(e x − 1), α = 1 a smooth negative side that saturates at −α, which pushes mean outputs towards zero (the paper's argument for faster learning); costs an exponential Clevert, Unterthiner and Hochreiter 2015 SELU λα(e x − 1), and λ x for x > 0; λ ≈ 1.0507, α ≈ 1.6733 constants chosen so that mean 0 and variance 1 is a fixed point of a layer with LeCun initialisation: the network normalises itself without BatchNorm, in fully connected networks Klambauer et al.
label: core

text: Dead units, measured A ReLU unit whose input is negative for every example outputs 0 everywhere and receives zero gradient, so nothing in backpropagation pushes it back: it is dead .
label: core
key: nothing in backpropagation pushes it back

text: A high learning rate or a large negative bias can kill many at once.
label: core
key: large negative bias can kill many at once

text: The usual statement is that a dead unit "never recovers".
label: core

text: That is exact only for a unit whose inputs cannot change (the first layer, fed fixed data); a dead unit deeper in the network can come back when the layers below it change, as the measured run below shows.
label: core
key: can come back when the layers below it change

label: core

label: core

text: Its expected value is x Φ( x ), so GELU is a deterministic version of a stochastic regulariser that blends ReLU (a mask of 0 or 1 set by the sign), dropout (a random 0) and zoneout (a random 1) ( GELU paper , section 2).

text: 2015 ) yes or no sigmoid BCEWithLogitsLoss , on the logit several yes/no labels at once one sigmoid per label BCEWithLogitsLoss , on the logits one class out of K softmax CrossEntropyLoss , on the logits the next token softmax over the vocabulary cross entropy on the logits in training; at generation the logits are divided by a temperature and filtered (top- k , top- p , min- p ) Softmax, in four facts.
label: core

text: (1) Adding a constant to every logit changes nothing, softmax( z + c ) = softmax( z ), which is why every implementation subtracts the largest logit before exponentiating (without it, e 1000 overflows).
label: core

text: (2) With two classes it is the sigmoid: softmax([ x , 0]) 1 = σ( x ) checked to 10 −15 , so a binary sigmoid output is a two-class softmax with one logit fixed at 0.
label: core

text: (3) Its derivative, ∂ p i /∂ z j = p i (δ ij − p j ), goes to zero as one probability approaches 1: a softmax saturates like a sigmoid, which is why it is paired with a log in the loss (cross entropy's gradient on the logits is simply p − y ).
label: core

text: (4) A temperature T , softmax( z / T ), sharpens ( T < 1) or flattens ( T > 1) the distribution without changing the order; try it on a real model's logits in the Sampler lab of Sampling and Decoding .
label: core

text: Softmax also normalises attention scores ( Attention Is All You Need ) and mixture-of-experts router scores.
label: core

text: Correction: with a large vocabulary, the cost is the projection, not the softmax The old page called softmax "expensive for very large K".
label: core

text: The exponentials are cheap; what grows with the vocabulary V is the output projection that produces the logits: d · V multiply-adds per token against V exponentials.
label: depth

text: For Qwen2.5-0.5B ( d = 896, V = 151,936, config.json ) that is 136 million multiply-adds against 152 thousand exponentials, 896 times more derived ; and in training the logits themselves take memory: a batch of 8 sequences of 4,096 tokens holds 8 × 4,096 × 151,936 = 5.0 billion logits, 19.9 GB in 32-bit floats derived .
label: depth

text: Sampled and hierarchical softmaxes, and fused or chunked cross-entropy kernels, target these two costs.
label: depth

text: Common mistakes Applying softmax (or sigmoid) before a loss that applies it again CrossEntropyLoss expects "the unnormalized logits for each class" ( PyTorch docs ); a softmax in front of it squashes the scores twice, so training still runs but the gradients are wrong and confidence is capped.
label: depth
key: the unnormalized logits for each class

text: End the network with logits and put the softmax only where probabilities are read.
label: depth
key: the unnormalized logits for each class

text: Sigmoid followed by BCELoss instead of BCEWithLogitsLoss The combined loss "is more numerically stable than using a plain Sigmoid followed by a BCELoss as, by combining the operations into one layer, we take advantage of the log-sum-exp trick for numerical stability" ( PyTorch docs ).
label: depth

text: A saturated sigmoid rounds to exactly 0 or 1, and the log of that is infinite.
label: depth

text: A ReLU or sigmoid on a regression output A ReLU output can never predict a negative value and receives no gradient when it outputs 0; a sigmoid caps it at 1.
